name: Course Plans and Graduation Audits
title: Course Plans and Graduation Audits
answer: Course plans and graduation audits are two linked counseling practices. A four year plan keeps a student's college, career, and trade options open, while an audit checks whether the student is actually on track to graduate. AI can help explore courses and flag missing requirements, but a counselor reviews and approves every plan and every flag.

sections.body: Course selection has long consequences, so a four year plan needs to include the courses that preserve later choices in college, careers, and trades. AI tools inside platforms such as Scoir and BigFuture can help students explore courses that match their interests and goals. Graduation audits serve a different but related purpose: they check whether a student is on track to graduate. Student information systems can run audits that mark missing credits or unmet requirements. The problem this solves is that a missed requirement can go unnoticed until it is hard to repair, while a counselor's review keeps the plan and the audit tied to the student's actual situation.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In high school, the work begins with a four year plan that maps courses against graduation requirements and the student's goals. AI tools in Scoir and BigFuture can help students explore options, and AI can help counselors map career and technical education and dual credit pathways so students and families understand them. Student information systems can run graduation audits that mark missing credits or unmet requirements. A counselor reviews each flag, because records may be wrong or may not include courses taken at another school. Catching a problem in junior year leaves time to fix it, and the counselor makes sure the plan meets graduation requirements and fits the student's goals.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The supplied text gives no evidence label, study, figure, or finding for course plans and graduation audits. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research as described here. The text presents the approach through the work of counselors and the use of AI tools in platforms such as Scoir and BigFuture, not through a cited study. It also refers to the algebra placement discussion in Chapter 7, but that reference is not an evidence claim in this passage.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The counselor reviews and approves every plan, and a counselor reviews each graduation audit flag. Records may be wrong or may not include courses taken at another school, so a flag is not a final judgment. Plans must reflect the student's own interests and potential rather than assumptions. A tool that suggests courses based on past grades might steer a student away from a challenge they could meet, so counselors should encourage students to take on challenge. Counselors should also look for patterns in who gets placed into advanced courses, and the book points to its algebra placement discussion in Chapter 7 as relevant here.
